finding: Test 17 asserts a retried unit "writes no path its failed attempt used", but §3.1 states the opposite for the only artifact a role unit writes: "A role's findings file is named by role rather than by `seq`, so a retry overwrites its own failed attempt" — and §3.3/§6.3 pin that path as `$TP_ROUND_DIR/$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson`. A test written to item 17 as phrased would fail the design §3.1 requires.
suggestion: Rewrite item 17 to match §3.1: a retried unit gets a fresh `seq` and therefore a fresh *log* path, while its durable artifact path is unchanged and the retry overwrites the failed attempt's file; the record unit then merges exactly one file per role.

finding: With the per-attempt seq prefix removed, the durable-write predicate for review-role/audit-role ('$TP_ROUND_DIR/$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson exists') is satisfied by a file the *previous failed attempt* left behind. §3.3 argues the predicates are safe because each is 'a state, never a delta' with 'no baseline', but that argument held only while the filename was unique per attempt: now the Stop hook (§6.2) lets a retried role unit stop having written nothing, and the record unit merges the failed attempt's partial file as if it were the round's result.
suggestion: Either state that the driver deletes $TP_ROUND_DIR/$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson before spawning each attempt of a role unit (making existence again mean 'this attempt wrote it'), or make the role unit write atomically (temp + rename) and say so, so a partial file can never exist.

finding: `interrupted` is one of the eight `stop_reason` rows and is the only one with no test. Test 3 covers 'each cap produces its own stop_reason' (interrupted is not a cap), 21 covers escalation, 7 covers no-units, 8/21 cover unit-failure. The three observable claims in §3.4's signal paragraph — SIGINT and SIGTERM set `interrupted`, in-flight children finish rather than being killed, and the run state is written before the driver exits — are all testable with the fake runner and none are pinned. The adjoining claim that caps are evaluated between iterations only, so a run overshoots by at most one iteration and 'the driver kills nothing', is likewise untested.
suggestion: Add a §10.1 item: 'SIGINT and SIGTERM each stop the run with `interrupted`: the in-flight child is allowed to exit (its run.json row is completed, not left null), no further unit is spawned, and `.tp/run-<base>.json` carries `stop_reason: interrupted` when the driver exits. A cap crossed mid-iteration lets the already-spawned children finish and overshoots by at most one iteration.'

finding: For a round-based phase the spec never says whether `next_units` omits roles whose findings file already exists in `$TP_ROUND_DIR`. §3.1 justifies the cycle-keyed round directory by saying an interrupted round "keeps the role files it already collected and the next run's record unit merges the completed set" — which only pays off if the second run re-runs just the missing roles — while test 36 says "a re-run role overwrites its own file rather than adding one", which reads as all roles re-running. The oracle cannot be built until this is pinned: it determines whether `tp resume` must stat `$TP_ROUND_DIR` (and therefore derive that path itself, which today only the driver does) before emitting the array.
suggestion: State the rule in §4.1: e.g. "in a round-based phase `next_units` contains one role unit per active role whose `$TP_ROUND_DIR/<role>.ndjson` is absent; when all are present the array holds the record unit" — and make test 36 assert that shape rather than a re-run.

finding: §4.1 says `next_units` "is the machine surface, and the only field the driver parses", but the same paragraph requires the driver to parse `round` and `phase` ("`round` and the existing `phase` are what the driver substitutes into `TP_ROUND` and `TP_ROUND_DIR`"), §4.1's releasable test reads `phase` == `release`, and §3.5's `--status` reports phase. The claim contradicts three other consumers in the spec, and test 38 (§10.5) pins `next_units` plus `round` together.
suggestion: Restate as: the driver parses exactly `phase`, `round` and `next_units` from `tp resume --json`, and nothing else (in particular never `next_action`'s prose). Keep `next_units` as "the only unit-selection surface" rather than "the only field parsed".

finding: §4.1 still claims next_units 'is the machine surface, and the only field the driver parses', but the same paragraph now requires the driver to read `round` (and `phase`) to substitute TP_ROUND and TP_ROUND_DIR. Round 6's addition of `round` invalidated the sentence it was inserted next to; a driver implementer reading the old claim will not parse the field the new sentence depends on.
suggestion: Restate as: next_units, round and phase are the machine surface the driver parses; next_action is human-facing and never parsed.

finding: The §5.1 fence covers `--skip-gate`, round budgets, `import --force` and `run_max_*`, but §7 makes `runner` and `notify_cmd` ordinary workflow fields. `runner.cmd`/`args` and `notify_cmd` are arbitrary commands the *driver* executes; a unit that runs `tp set --workflow runner=…` (a supported route, not a shell edit) changes what the driver spawns for every later unit of the same run, and does so by writing `.tp/config.json` — exactly the file §6.2 denies to the editing tools. This is a larger hatch than raising a cap, which §5.1 calls the thing the fence exists to close.
suggestion: Add `runner` and `notify_cmd` to the §5.1 table as user-only under `TP_UNATTENDED` (exit 2, same hint shape), and add a §10.3 case asserting it. If they must stay settable, say why executing an agent-authored command is acceptable where raising a cap is not.

finding: §5.2 pins five separate `notify_cmd` behaviours — invoked on *every* non-converged stop (not escalation alone), exec'd without a shell, split on whitespace, given `TP_STOP_REASON`/`TP_RUN_ID`/(on escalation)`TP_ESCALATION_PATH`, and its exit code reported but never changing `stop_reason`. Test 21 asserts only that an escalating unit 'invokes `notify_cmd` when configured'. The four remaining claims — including the negative one that most needs pinning (a failing `notify_cmd` must not alter the run's outcome) — have no test, and the no-shell/whitespace-split claim is exactly the kind two engineers implement differently.
suggestion: Add a §10.3 item: '`notify_cmd` fires on each non-converged stop_reason (cap, unit-failure, no-units, interrupted, escalation) and not on `converged`; it is exec'd without a shell (a value containing shell metacharacters is passed as literal argv, not interpreted) split on whitespace; it receives TP_STOP_REASON and TP_RUN_ID, plus TP_ESCALATION_PATH only on escalation; and a notify_cmd exiting non-zero leaves stop_reason and the run state unchanged.'

finding: The Stop hook must decide whether "the durable write is the state that kind names in §3.3's fourth column", but the spec gives it no way to compute that. The eight predicates include reading a task's `status` out of `$TP_FILE`, checking that a review/audit round file exists for `$TP_ROUND`, and — for `review-resolve` — that *every* finding in the round's file carries a disposition. A shipped hook is a shell/script entry with a 10s timeout (§6.4) and is explicitly forbidden to read the run state (§6.2), so the implementer must reimplement JSON parsing of the task file, the `.tp-review/` round files and the disposition rule inside the hook — a second implementation of driver logic that will drift from it, which is exactly the two-sources-of-truth failure §3.5 argues against.
suggestion: Specify one tp command the hook and the driver both call — e.g. `tp unit --check` (or `tp run --check-unit`) reading `TP_UNIT_KIND`/`TP_UNIT_ID`/`TP_ROUND_DIR`/`TP_FILE` and exiting 0 when the durable write is present, 1 when absent, 2 on a missing/unknown kind — and state that §3.3's fourth column is implemented once, there.

finding: §6.3 declares `tp-implementer`, `tp-reviewer` and `tp-auditor` with per-role tool restrictions, but no section wires an agent to a unit. §3.2.1's `claude` template args are fixed (`-p`, `--output-format`, `--verbose`, `--permission-mode auto`) with no agent selector, §3.2's placeholder set has none either, and §3.3 says each kind's brief comes from `brief_command` only. Five of the eight kinds (`review-record`, `review-resolve`, `decompose`, `audit-record`, `audit-fix`) also have no agent at all. As written the restrictions can never take effect through the driver's own spawn path, yet §6.2/§6.3 lean on them as the enforcement half of the scope fence.
suggestion: Either state the selection mechanism (e.g. the per-kind `{prompt}` names the agent to delegate to, or the `claude` template appends an agent flag driven by `TP_UNIT_KIND`), and give the kind→agent mapping for all eight kinds; or say explicitly that the agents are for interactive/plugin use only and that unattended units get their restrictions from the hooks in §6.2 alone.

finding: §6.4 is normative in full ("Every hook the plugin ships declares a `timeout` of 10 seconds and exits non-zero rather than hanging") and §10 contains no test for it — §10.4's four items cover validation, the deny matcher, the Stop hook's escalation branch and TP_ROUND_DIR, none of which observe a timeout or the non-zero-on-timeout exit. §2's prior-art row names hooks recursing without timeout as the failure this section answers, so the one claim that answers a catalogued failure is the one with no pass/fail test.
suggestion: Add to §10.4: 'Every shipped hook declares timeout 10 in its plugin manifest (assert the parsed value for each hook entry), and a hook whose helper exceeds its budget exits non-zero rather than hanging (assert exit status and bounded elapsed time with a stub that sleeps past the timeout).'

finding: §7 places the new fields in the precedence chain "CLI > env > task override > project config > built-in" and §5.1 requires that "under the variable the env layer of §7's precedence is ignored for every fenced field", with test 40 asserting it. But no environment variable name is given for any workflow field, new or existing, and the only TP_* variables the codebase reads are `TP_FILE` and `TP_HC` — neither a workflow field. An implementer therefore has to invent the naming scheme (`TP_RUN_MAX_UNITS`? `TP_WORKFLOW_RUN_MAX_UNITS`?), the parse/validation behaviour for a malformed value, and the exact set of "fenced fields" the exclusion covers (`run_max_*` and the two round budgets only, or `runner`/`notify_cmd` too), before §5.1's guarantee or test 40 can be written at all.
suggestion: Add to §7 a table row or sentence naming the env variable for each workflow field (e.g. `TP_<FIELD_UPPER>`), the behaviour on an unparseable value, and an explicit list of the fields §5.1 fences; if no env layer is intended for these fields, drop `env` from the sentence and restate test 40 against whatever layer it does apply to.

finding: The restated arity claim asserts that 'which kind of 2 it is, a refusal (§5.1) or a typo, is carried by the escalation record's presence (§5.2)'. §5.2 makes the record a *separate voluntary action* — a unit must run `tp escalate` to produce one — so a unit that hits a §5.1 refusal and exits carries no record, and is indistinguishable from a typo by exactly the signal §8a nominates. The same paragraph's rule that exit 2 uniformly means 'tp did not run the request' is also contradicted by `tp escalate`, which exits 2 after successfully performing what it was asked to do.
suggestion: Drop the escalation-record claim and disambiguate at the source: have §5.1's refusals carry a stable machine-readable marker (e.g. a `refusal` field / fixed hint code in the JSON error payload), and note that `tp escalate`'s exit 2 is a deliberate signalling exit, not a 'did not run' exit.

finding: Test 15 requires four paths to be git-ignored (`.tp/run-<base>.json`, `.tp/runs/`, `.tp/rounds/`, `.tp/last_failure-<base>.json`) while §10.6 says "The `.tp/.gitignore` fixture gains three entries". Neither list includes `.tp/locks/`, which §3.1 introduces as the run lock's home (`.tp/locks/run-<base>.lock`) — a per-run artifact that would otherwise be committed.
suggestion: Make the two statements agree on one list, and add `.tp/locks/` to it unless that directory is already ignored by an existing entry (say so if it is).

finding: §10.6 claims "no other command's exit codes change outside `TP_UNATTENDED=1`", but §8a changes `tp review --merge` and `tp audit --merge` from always-exit-0 to exit 1 when an input has lines and none parsed — an exit-code change on two commands, outside unattended mode, that existing merge tests will pin. §10.6 also omits the `file_summary` shape change (§8a adds `truncated` and `total_changed`) that current audit-payload assertions pin.
suggestion: Add both to §10.6: merge tests asserting exit 0 on a malformed-input fixture move in the same task as the `inputs` change, and `file_summary` assertions move with the truncation change. Then reword the closing sentence so it no longer claims exhaustiveness it does not have.

finding: Round 6 made `round` null outside a round-based phase, but §3.1 still spawns every child with TP_ROUND and TP_ROUND_DIR and defines TP_ROUND_DIR as '.tp/rounds/<base>/<phase>-r$TP_ROUND'. For implement and decompose units round is null, so neither variable has a defined value — the path would render as '...-r' or '...-rnull'. Test 37 compounds this by asserting every child receives all eight variables 'with their documented forms'.
suggestion: State what happens when round is null: either both variables are unset for non-round phases (and say the Stop hook and role paths are then unused), or give them an explicit documented value; then qualify test 37 to the round-based phases for those two variables.

finding: Unit ids become path components — `$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl` (§3.5) and `$TP_ROUND_DIR/$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson` (§3.3, §6.3) — but §3.1 defines an `audit-fix` id as the finding's `role:item_id`, and an `item_id` is agent-authored text that can contain `/`, spaces, `§` or a leading `.`. There is no sanitization, length or collision rule, so the driver can be made to write outside `$TP_RUN_DIR`, and the §6.3 allowlist ("may write exactly one path") cannot be expressed against an unsanitized name.
suggestion: Define the path encoding for unit ids once: e.g. path components are the id with every character outside `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` replaced by `-`, truncated to N bytes with a short hash suffix, rejecting empty results — and note that `$TP_UNIT_ID` in the environment stays the raw id while the file name uses the encoded form.

finding: §4.1 states `round` is 'null outside a round-based phase', and §3.1 requires `TP_ROUND` and `TP_ROUND_DIR` in every child's environment with `TP_ROUND_DIR` = `.tp/rounds/<base>/<phase>-r$TP_ROUND`. The spec never says what those two variables hold when `round` is null (implement and decompose units): unset, empty, the literal `null`, or a directory ending in `-r`. Test 37 asks for '`TP_ROUND_DIR` derived from phase and round' for every child, which cannot be asserted for an `implement` unit until that case is pinned — and §6.2's Stop hook reads `$TP_RUN_DIR/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-escalation.json` while role predicates read `$TP_ROUND_DIR`, so a wrong choice silently mis-resolves paths.
suggestion: State in §3.1 that when `round` is null both `TP_ROUND` and `TP_ROUND_DIR` are absent from the child's environment (not empty strings), and extend test 37: 'an `implement` or `decompose` child has neither variable set; a role or record child has both, with `TP_ROUND_DIR` = `.tp/rounds/<base>/<phase>-r<round>`.'

finding: The per-kind runner map is a first-class shape with three normative rules and no test: 'a map from unit kind to either of those with a `default` key covering the rest', 'A map missing `default` is a usage error' (§3.2), and 'Under a per-kind map the cap accrues only the reporting kinds, and the run-start report names which kinds are unmetered' (§3.2.2). Test 10 covers placeholders, test 11 covers a single runner declaring no `spend_key`. Nothing pins that a per-kind map dispatches the right cmd per kind, that a missing `default` exits 2, or that a mixed metered/unmetered run reports which kinds are unmetered rather than presenting a partial total as complete — the exact misreading §3.2.2 says it exists to prevent.
suggestion: Add to §10.2: 'A per-kind `runner` map dispatches each kind to its own cmd and falls back to `default`; a map without `default` is a usage error (exit 2) before any child is spawned; and under a map where only some kinds declare `spend_key`, `cap-budget` accrues only those kinds and the run-start report names the unmetered kinds by name.'

finding: Two spawn-contract claims stated as required behaviour have no test: 'Every child is spawned with stdin closed' (§3.2.1, cited in §2's prior-art table as the fix for backgrounded runs hanging on stdin) and 'Children are spawned in the repository root' (§3.1). Both are deterministically observable through the `TP_RUNNER` fake — a fake that reads stdin sees EOF, and one that prints its cwd can be compared against the repo root — yet §10.1/§10.2 assert neither, so the hardest-to-diagnose unattended failure named in the spec has no regression guard.
suggestion: Add to §10.2: 'A child spawned by the driver has stdin closed (the fake runner's read of stdin returns EOF immediately) and runs with the repository root as its working directory, whatever directory `tp run` was invoked from.'

finding: "the driver reads one number from the final line of that unit's log" has no error path, yet every failure mode of an unattended run produces one: an empty log (spawn or auth failed before output), a final line that is not JSON (a crash message), a valid final line without the `spend_key`, or a non-numeric value. Nothing says whether the unit's `spend_usd` becomes null, whether the run's accrued total is still trustworthy for `cap-budget`, and whether a parse failure is itself a unit failure.
suggestion: Add one sentence: a missing/unparseable final line or absent key records `spend_usd: null` for that unit, never fails the unit, and is reported once in `--status` so a partial `cap-budget` total is not read as complete (the same honesty §3.2.2 already applies to unmetered kinds).

finding: "The driver decides a unit succeeded from its exit code and from re-reading cycle state" leaves the two signals' combination undefined for the cases that actually occur. Exit 0 with the durable write absent (an agent that stopped early — precisely what §6.2's Stop hook exists to catch, and which the hook only blocks *once*) and exit non-zero with the durable write present (the unit did the work and then failed a cleanup command) both need a stated verdict, because that verdict drives the retry counter, `last_failure` (§4.2, keyed on non-zero exit only) and `unit-failure`.
suggestion: State the success predicate as a conjunction and name both mixed cases: e.g. "a unit succeeded iff it exited 0 *and* its §3.3 durable write is present; any other combination is a failed attempt, and a non-zero exit with the write present is still a failure" — then align §4.2's `last_failure` trigger with it.

finding: Seven of the eight durable-write predicates are scoped to the unit's own subject (`$TP_UNIT_ID`, `$TP_ROUND`, that finding's row). `decompose`'s is not: "The task file holds at least one task". A decompose unit that imports 1 of 13 tasks, or that crashes after a partial import and is retried, satisfies the predicate — so both the Stop hook (§6.2) and the driver's success test (§3.3) pass a decomposition that is not done, and §7's phase advance then rests on it.
suggestion: Scope the predicate to something the unit alone can newly satisfy — e.g. the task file's coverage validating clean (`tp validate` exit 0), or a decompose marker written by the import — so a partial import fails the same way a partial implement does.

finding: Two of the eight durable-write predicates are stated in terms the spec never defines, so test 18 ('each durable-write predicate is decidable from one file') cannot be written the same way twice. `review-resolve`: 'Every finding in the round's file carries a disposition' — `disposition` appears exactly once in the spec, with no field name and no set of accepted values. `audit-fix`: 'That finding's row is recorded resolved' — no field name or status value either. The Stop hook (§6.2) blocks on precisely these predicates, so an ambiguous predicate is also an ambiguous block/allow decision.
suggestion: Name the field and accepted values for both rows, e.g. 'every finding object in the round file has a non-empty `resolution` field' and 'the finding's row in the round file has `status` in {resolved, wontfix}', so §10.2 item 18 and the §6.2 hook assert one literal condition.

finding: "A unit is attempted `1 + run_max_unit_retries` times" fixes the count but not the mechanics, and §3.1's six-step loop has no retry step. Unspecified: whether a retry happens inside the same iteration or after re-reading cycle state and re-polling `next_units` (step 5/6 could legitimately return a different unit set); whether a failure in one of N concurrent role units retries only that role or the whole batch; and whether the attempt counter is per `(kind,id)` for the life of the run or reset when the unit reappears in a later iteration. Each choice yields a different driver.
suggestion: Extend §3.1's loop with the retry step and state the scope explicitly: retries are per `(kind,id)`, attempted within the same iteration, only the failing member of a concurrent batch is retried, and the attempt counter persists for the whole run.

finding: "`SIGINT` and `SIGTERM` set `interrupted` on the same terms: in-flight children finish" cannot hold for the ordinary case of an operator pressing Ctrl-C: the terminal delivers SIGINT to the whole foreground process group, so children receive it too and die mid-write. The promise only works if the driver puts each child in its own process group (`Setpgid`), and that is nowhere stated — nor is what the driver does with a child that dies from the same signal (failed attempt? not counted?).
suggestion: State that children are spawned in their own process group so a terminal signal reaches the driver only, and say how a child killed by a signal is classified (not a failed attempt, run stops with `interrupted`).

finding: §3.4 says caps are evaluated between iterations only and that "a run can overshoot its wall-clock and budget caps by at most one iteration", but the same rule applies to `run_max_units`: one iteration fans out one child per active role (§3.3), so an iteration starting at `run_max_units - 1` spawns the whole role set and overshoots the unit cap by roles-1. `cap-units` is described as "Spawned children reached `run_max_units`" with no overshoot allowance, and test 33 pins `run_max_units`, `totals.units` and `--status` to the same attempt count.
suggestion: Either include `cap-units` in the overshoot sentence (overshoot bounded by the largest concurrent unit set), or state that the driver truncates the spawned set when the remaining unit budget is smaller than the iteration's unit count — and say which, since §3.3 forbids splitting a role fan-out across iterations only implicitly.

finding: Two mechanisms are described for the same file and neither is made authoritative. §3.5 says "Each unit's runner output streams to `$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl`", implying the driver redirects the child's stdout; §3.2 offers a `{log_path}` placeholder, implying the runner writes the file itself. The `claude` template's args do not use `{log_path}`, so redirection must exist — but then a runner whose args *do* use `{log_path}` would have the driver redirecting into a file the child also opens. Spend reading (§3.2.2) depends on which of the two produced the bytes.
suggestion: State that the driver always creates and redirects the child's stdout to the log path, and that `{log_path}` is informational only (the runner may reference it but must not write to it); or forbid redirection when `{log_path}` appears in `args` and say which side then owns the file.

finding: §3.1's unification of the audit-fix id as `role:item_id` puts a colon — and whatever characters an auditor put in item_id — into two path templates that were previously fed only task ids and base names: the log path '$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl' (§3.5) and, indirectly, anything else keyed on unit id. No sanitization or escaping rule is given, so an item_id containing '/', a space, or a colon produces a broken or unexpected path in an unattended run nobody is watching.
suggestion: Add one sentence to §3.5: ids are slugified for path use (non [A-Za-z0-9._-] replaced with '-') while the run-state row keeps the unquoted id, so the durable id and the filesystem-safe id are stated once and never confused.

finding: Whether `round` is a top-level field of `tp resume --json` or a member of each next_units entry is not decidable from the text. §4.1 reads 'an ordered array ... each carrying {kind, id, brief_command}, alongside round', while test 38 reads '`next_units` carries {kind, id, brief_command} plus round' — which parses as per-entry. The section is otherwise precise about per-entry vs per-phase placement (it explicitly says concurrency 'is not repeated per entry'), so the omission is load-bearing for the parser.
suggestion: Name the placement explicitly, e.g. 'a sibling top-level field `round` on the resume payload, not repeated per entry, since every unit in one array belongs to one round', and align test 38's wording with it.

finding: §4.1 names two distinct conditions that produce `next_units: []` on a non-releasable cycle — 'a phase whose work is blocked, and a phase awaiting an operator decision' — and adds that '`next_action.summary` names what the phase is waiting for'. Test 7 covers only the generic case (empty array stops with `no-units` on the first iteration). Neither branch is constructed by a test, and the `summary` claim is both untested and unfalsifiable as written ('names what the phase is waiting for' admits any non-empty string).
suggestion: Split test 7: '(a) a phase whose only tasks are dependency-blocked and (b) a phase awaiting an operator decision each return `next_units: []` and stop the run with `no-units`; in each case `next_action.summary` is non-empty and contains the blocking task id / the decision name respectively.'

finding: §4.2 gives `last_failure` two triggers — 'When a unit exits non-zero, **or closes with a failed quality gate**' — and a six-field shape `{unit_kind, unit_id, phase, exit_code, summary, at}` whose `summary` must carry 'the gate's own output when a gate failed' and never the child's prose. Test 23 exercises only the non-zero-exit trigger and asserts nothing about the field set or `summary`'s provenance. The gate-failure path is the one that can occur while the unit exits zero, so it is the branch a driver test would otherwise never reach.
suggestion: Extend test 23: 'A unit whose `tp done` fails the quality gate writes `last_failure` even when the child exits zero; the record carries all six documented fields, `exit_code` reflects the gate failure, and `summary` contains the failing command and gate output rather than any text the child printed.'

finding: The env-layer fence over-corrects relative to the rule it was added to enforce. §5.1 permits an equal or lower value ('lowering a budget cannot manufacture convergence'), yet ignoring the env layer wholesale also discards a *lower* env-supplied cap, silently resolving to a higher value than the operator's environment asked for — the opposite of failing closed, and with no diagnostic. It also makes the same command resolve different values inside and outside a run with nothing reported.
suggestion: Fence the direction, not the layer: under TP_UNATTENDED an env value above the otherwise-resolved value is ignored (and reported once at run start), while an equal or lower env value still applies — matching the CLI refusal rule in the same table.

finding: §5.1 defines unattended mode with a three-way rule — 'active when the variable is present, non-empty and not `0`' — but every test uses only the two extremes: test 19 uses `TP_UNATTENDED=1` and 'without the variable', test 40 uses `=1`. The two boundary values that separate the rule from a simple presence check, `TP_UNATTENDED=` (empty) and `TP_UNATTENDED=0`, are untested, so an implementation that treats presence alone as active passes every listed test while contradicting the spec.
suggestion: Extend test 19 with the activation matrix: 'unset, empty and `0` leave the four operations exiting 0; `1`, `true` and any other non-empty non-`0` value make them exit 2.'

finding: §8a establishes that exit 2 means uniformly "tp did not run the request" and exit 1 means "it ran and failed". `tp escalate` (§5.2) contradicts that on its success path: it validates its arguments, writes its record, and exits 2 — the request ran and produced its intended durable artifact. A driver that branches on §8a's rule would classify a successful escalation as a request tp refused to run, which is exactly the ambiguity §8a exists to remove.
suggestion: Either state the exception explicitly in §8a (`tp escalate`'s 2 is the escalation signal, disambiguated by the record's presence, as §8a already hints for refusals), or give escalation its own exit code and keep §8a's rule unqualified.

finding: "The plugin instead preflights: if `tp` is absent from `PATH` or older than `0.35.0`, it fails with the install command" names no host: which hook event runs it (SessionStart is specified as carrying `tp resume --compact` "and nothing else"), what "fails" means to the client (non-zero exit, blocking JSON, or context text), and how the version is compared — `tp --version` output format, and the verdict for a dev/`-dirty` build or a non-semver string — are all left to the implementer, while §6.4 requires every hook to be bounded at 10s.
suggestion: Pin the preflight to a named event and channel (e.g. a `SessionStart` step that emits an additional-context line and exits 0, or a blocking exit 2 with the install command on stderr), state the `tp --version` parse rule, and say that an unparseable version is treated as satisfying the minimum rather than blocking the session.

finding: §6.1's preflight is normative and precise — 'if `tp` is absent from `PATH` or older than `0.35.0`, it fails with the install command rather than degrading quietly', with the minimum taken from `plugin.json`'s own version and compared against `tp --version` — and §10.4 has no test for it. Test 24 covers `claude plugin validate` and hook fixtures only. Both branches (absent binary, older binary) and the equal-version boundary are mechanically testable by stubbing `tp --version` on PATH.
suggestion: Add to §10.4: 'With `tp` absent from PATH the preflight fails and its message contains the install command; with `tp --version` reporting a version below `plugin.json`'s the preflight fails the same way; with exactly that version, and with a higher one, it passes.'

finding: §6.2 says the Stop hook's durable write is "the state that kind names in §3.3's fourth column". §3.3's columns are Kind | Ends in | Durable write | Concurrency — the durable write is the **third** column; the fourth is Concurrency. A hook implemented against the literal reference reads the wrong column, and the Stop hook is the one component §3.3 explicitly requires to read the same predicate as the driver.
suggestion: Say "§3.3's `Durable write` column" rather than an ordinal, so the reference survives any future column insertion.

finding: §6.3's central claim — 'The reviewer and auditor may write exactly one path — their own findings file at `$TP_ROUND_DIR/$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson` — and are denied every other write' — has no test. Test 27 covers only that `tp review`/`tp audit` emit that path under `TP_ROUND_DIR` and that the record unit merges the directory; test 25 covers the `PreToolUse` deny list, which is a different mechanism (four path patterns, not an allowlist of one). Also untested is the closing sentence 'Outside a run the emitted filename is unchanged', which is the regression guard for every existing non-run workflow.
suggestion: Extend test 27 or add to §10.4: 'The `tp-reviewer` and `tp-auditor` agent definitions permit a write to `$TP_ROUND_DIR/$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson` and deny a write to any other path (assert against the parsed definition); and with `TP_ROUND_DIR` unset, `tp review`/`tp audit` emit the pre-0.35.0 filename unchanged.'

finding: 'Under `--compact`, `stop_reason` and the cap totals survive; per-unit rows and log paths are stripped' is a concrete field-level output contract with no test. Test 14 covers `tp run --status` in its full form only, and §10.2's list never mentions `--compact`. This is a P3-relevant claim (compact output is what an agent reads) and is the easiest kind of assertion to write, so its absence is a straightforward gap rather than a judgement call.
suggestion: Add to §10.2: '`tp run --status --compact` keeps `stop_reason` and `totals` (units, wall_clock_seconds, spend_usd) and contains no `units[]` rows and no `log_path` key, for both an in-flight and a stopped run.'

finding: '`tp config --resolved`, `tp config --extract` and `tp validate --project` cover the new fields on the same terms as every existing workflow field' is a required behaviour with no test. Test 16 covers defaults, ranges, precedence and `notify_cmd`'s source, but names none of these three commands. This is the exact defect v0.31.1 shipped a fix for — a workflow field missing from `--extract`/`validate --project` — and the fix was made durable by a config-assertion guard test, which this spec does not ask for while adding seven new fields.
suggestion: Add to §10.2: 'Each of the seven §7 fields appears in `tp config --resolved`, round-trips through `tp config --extract`, and is validated by `tp validate --project` (an out-of-range value in `.tp/config.json` is reported), asserted by enumerating the field set rather than spot-checking one field.'

finding: `notify_cmd` is exec'd by the driver (§5.2) and read from `.tp/local.json` only, but no command is specified that writes it — `tp use` writes the active pointer and flag defaults, and §6.2 denies the editing tools any write to `.tp/local.json`, so on a fresh machine there is no stated route to configure it at all. The same gap has a safety edge: `notify_cmd` is not among §5.1's fenced decisions, so if any tp command can set it, an unattended unit can choose a command the driver will execute outside the fence.
suggestion: Name the write path (e.g. `tp config --local notify_cmd=...`) and either add `notify_cmd` to §5.1's fenced set under `TP_UNATTENDED`, or state explicitly that setting it is refused in unattended mode.

finding: §7 enumerates the precedence exceptions exhaustively — 'with two exceptions: notify_cmd ... and TP_RUNNER' — but round 6 added a third in §5.1: under TP_UNATTENDED the env layer is ignored for every fenced field. §7 is the section a reader consults for resolution order, so the fence is invisible where it matters, and §7's list is now false as written.
suggestion: Add the third exception to §7 and define 'fenced field' in one place (review_max_rounds, audit_max_rounds, run_max_*), referencing §5.1 rather than restating the rule.

finding: §7's `runner` row gives the range as 'Built-in name or object', but §3.2 defines three legal shapes — built-in template name, runner object, or a per-kind map. A test written from §7 rejects a per-kind map as out of range; a test written from §3.2 accepts it. The same row, plus `notify_cmd` ('Any command string'), also breaks test 16's rule 'accepts both range endpoints and rejects one step outside each': neither has endpoints, so 'one step outside' is undefined and the test cannot be written for two of the seven rows.
suggestion: Make the `runner` range read 'Built-in name, runner object, or per-kind map with `default`', and scope test 16's endpoint clause to the five numeric fields, replacing it for `runner`/`notify_cmd` with the named invalid cases (unknown built-in name, map without `default`, empty string) and their exit codes.

finding: The dropped-role rule turns on a boundary: '`--merge` exit 1 when an input has at least one line, none of which parsed', while a zero-byte file exits 0. Test 32 pins both ends (all-lines-fail → 1, all-inputs-zero-byte → 0) but not the case in between — an input where some lines parse and some are skipped — which must still exit 0 with a non-zero `skipped` count. That is the case an implementation naively written as 'skipped > 0 → exit 1' gets wrong, and it is also what makes the `{path, parsed, skipped}` triple worth reporting at all.
suggestion: Extend test 32: 'an input with 3 parsed and 2 skipped lines exits 0, reports parsed 3 / skipped 2, and its parsed rows appear in the merged set; only an input with parsed 0 and skipped > 0 exits 1.'

finding: `location_clusters` is justified by a driver-facing failure — "a human reads that as 'more to do'; an unattended driver reads it as rounds remaining" — but no unattended consumer ever sees it. §4.1 makes `next_units` "the only field the driver parses", Non-Goal 6 forbids inferring anything else from a unit's output, and §3.5 streams every unit's stdout to a log the driver "never reads into any context". §3.5's `tp run --status` surfaces `spec_coverage_clean_rounds`/`role_streaks`/`divergence` on an audit-phase stop but carries no review-phase counterpart, so on a review-phase stop the clustered counts reach neither the driver nor the operator. What the release actually adds is bytes on every `tp review --merge`/`--status` payload for an interactive reader — and on `--merge` those bytes restate a grouping that is a pure function of the finding rows already in the same payload (role, location, severity per row).
suggestion: Route the signal to where the unattended path can read it: have §3.5's `tp run --status` carry `location_clusters` (and the review convergence counters) on a review-phase stop, mirroring the audit-phase divergence block that §1 promises. Additionally pin `--compact` behaviour for the new key — it is derivable from the merged rows, so `--compact` should strip it — or, if the field is meant for a human at a terminal only, say so and drop the unattended-driver framing that currently earns it.

finding: Test 24's second half, 'its hook payloads are asserted against fixtures', names neither which payloads nor which hooks. Three hooks ship with materially different payloads (§6.2: SessionStart injects `tp resume --compact` 'and nothing else'; PreToolUse returns a deny decision; Stop returns a block-with-reason), and only the SessionStart bound is stated in prose. As written, one engineer fixtures all three payload shapes and another fixtures one, and the §6.2 claim that the SessionStart payload is exactly `tp resume --compact` output has no dedicated assertion.
suggestion: Split test 24: 'The plugin validates with `claude plugin validate`; the SessionStart hook's injected context equals `tp resume --compact`'s output and contains nothing else; the PreToolUse deny payload and the Stop block payload each match a checked-in fixture including the reason field.'

finding: Test 29 — '`next_action`'s mechanize branch carries the phase qualifier' — is not a deterministic assertion: §8a specifies the qualifier's content ('it names the class and states that a check is worth registering only when the artifact it measures already exists in the review phase') but no field, no literal substring and no structured flag, so two engineers assert on two different strings and either passes. The companion doc changes (SKILL.md's mechanize-candidate rule, Workflow D step 3) are likewise stated as required 'in the same task' with no check.
suggestion: Pin the observable: name the field the qualifier occupies (e.g. `next_action.payload.mechanize.phase_note`) or a required literal substring, and have test 29 assert that field's presence and that it names the candidate class, for a cycle with a third-round mechanize candidate.

finding: Test 37 pins 'the eight documented environment variables', matching §3.1's list, but §5.1 sets a ninth on every child (TP_UNATTENDED=1, after the runner.env merge). A test written to the literal count asserts the incomplete set, and the one variable whose presence gates every §5.1 refusal is the one omitted.
suggestion: Drop the literal count or make it nine and include TP_UNATTENDED, cross-referencing §5.1 — test 20 only covers that runner.env cannot override it, not that it is present.

finding: The exact `.tp/.gitignore` lines are never given, and the two places that describe them disagree in count: test 15 names four artifacts (`.tp/run-<base>.json`, `.tp/runs/`, `.tp/rounds/`, `.tp/last_failure-<base>.json`) while §10.6 says "The `.tp/.gitignore` fixture gains three entries". Since two of the four are per-base and must be written as globs, the implementer has to guess both the pattern form and how many lines the fixture assertion expects.
suggestion: Write the literal lines into §3.5 (e.g. `run-*.json`, `last_failure-*.json`, `runs/`, `rounds/`) and correct §10.6's count to match.

finding: `{unit_id}` and `{unit_kind}` are documented operator-facing placeholders in §3.2's `args` row, yet neither shipped template uses them (§3.2.1: `claude` uses `{prompt}` and `{max_budget_usd}`, `opencode` only `{prompt}`), and §3.1 already gives every child `TP_UNIT_ID` and `TP_UNIT_KIND` in its environment. Their only named consumer is the `TP_RUNNER` fake seam's arg list. The result is a widened config surface — one an operator must read and tp must validate and error on (unresolved placeholder ⇒ exit 2) — carried for a test seam that already receives the same two values another way.
suggestion: Either name the real runner shape that must take unit id/kind on argv (as `{log_path}` plausibly has: a runner that redirects its own output), or drop the two from §3.2's placeholder table and have the fake runner read `TP_UNIT_ID`/`TP_UNIT_KIND` from the environment it is already spawned with, leaving `{prompt}`, `{max_budget_usd}` and `{log_path}` as the documented set.

finding: The log path is `$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl`, and §3.1 makes `<id>` a `role:item_id` pair for `audit-fix` and a task id or spec base name elsewhere — values that can contain `:`, `/` or other characters that are not path-safe, none of which the spec says are escaped or sanitized. Test 17 ('writes no path its failed attempt used') and test 14 (reports 'the last unit's log path') both assume the path is well-formed, so neither would catch an `audit-fix` id that produces a nested or invalid filename.
suggestion: State the sanitization rule in §3.5 (e.g. every character outside `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` in `<id>` is replaced with `-` for the filename only, while `TP_UNIT_ID` carries the unescaped value) and add an assertion to test 17 that an `audit-fix` unit whose id contains `:` and `/` yields a single file directly under `$TP_RUN_DIR`.

finding: The log path is composed as `$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl` and the role artifact as `$TP_ROUND_DIR/$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson`, but §3.1 defines a unit's `id` as a durable subject whose grammar the spec never constrains — an `audit-fix` id is `role:item_id`, where `item_id` comes from an NDJSON row an audit sub-agent authored and may contain `/`, spaces or `..`. The spec pins the composition without pinning what may appear in it.
suggestion: State the id grammar (or the sanitization applied when an id becomes a path component) once in §3.1, and add a §10.2 case for an `audit-fix` id carrying a path separator.

finding: An escalating unit "is not counted as a failed attempt", which settles the retry counter but not the run counters: whether its spawn counts toward `run_max_units`, whether its row is appended to `units[]` and its spend accrued to `totals.spend_usd`. §3.4 says `totals.units`, `run_max_units` and `--status`'s units-done must all read the same number (test 33), so the escalation case has to be decided for all three at once.
suggestion: Add one clause: an escalating unit is a spawned attempt like any other — it appends its row, counts toward `run_max_units`/`totals.units` and accrues its spend — and only the retry counter ignores it.
